claims.text: On 1 October 2026 a SpaceX Falcon 9 lifted off from Vandenberg carrying 130 payloads [^7].
Hours later Google said it had "confirmed contact with the satellite and it is operating as expected" [^1].
The project's lead called the same flight "a very minimal test" [^6].
Four TPUs, reported as Trillium generation; Google's own posts give no chip count [^14,15]
SpaceX Falcon 9, Transporter-18 rideshare, Vandenberg SLC-4E; liftoff 11:32 a.m. PT on 1 Oct 2026 [^7]
Planet's CFO had already told investors in December 2025 that the work used Planet's Owl bus and that "a couple of demo satellites" were on contract [^11].
Planet counts it as its 40th launch, with 718 satellites built and delivered [^8].
The September 24 facts post sets out what the hardware had to survive first: roughly 10 minutes of launch, up to 10 g of sustained acceleration and component loads of 50 to 100 g.
Google SVP James Manyika told Engadget, "We don't expect … anything usefully operational in the next few years" [^14].
In November 2025 the stated plan was two prototype satellites by early 2027 [^3].
The ground baseline is unusually specific: Google put Trillium TPUs through a 67 MeV proton beam at UC Davis's Crocker Nuclear Laboratory and published per-rad error rates [^2,5].
The high-bandwidth memory began showing irregularities only after about 2 krad(Si), and one chip reached 15 krad(Si) without a hard failure.
The beam also logged soft errors, including 203 HBM uncorrectable-error events at about one per 44 rad.
The paper extrapolates silent data corruption to about one per 3 million inferences at one inference per second [^5].
By ARA's arithmetic, showing with 95% confidence that the crash (SEFI) rate is no worse than the ground estimate would take roughly 100 chip-years without an event.
HPE's Spaceborne Computer-1 on the ISS lost 9 of 20 SSDs and 1 of 4 power supplies, and needed 4 reboots, over about 1.6 years [^24].
A proton test of a 14 nm FinFET NXP system-on-chip projects 0.44–0.78 Linux crashes per year at 500 km, with 56% of errors in the filesystem and eMMC storage [^23].
NPR reported that the Gemma model will run "for 15 minutes at a time due to heat management constraints," and that radiators are among the heaviest components on the spacecraft [^6].
The International Space Station is the best-documented benchmark: its six radiator arrays reject about 70 kW [^18].
The whole ISS now generates more than 250 kW of solar power with its roll-out arrays, so a 1 GW cluster is about 4,000 space stations' worth of power [^19].
ARA's calculation for an ideal two-sided panel facing a 3 K sky, with emissivity 0.9, gives about 1.69 m² per kW at 276 K and 0.83 m² per kW at 330 K.
IEEE Spectrum's analysis puts the radiator for a single H100 at about 1.0 m² if the chip runs at 85 °C, 1.4 m² at 60 °C and roughly 3 m² at 20 °C [^20].
Rack scale compounds quickly: IEEE Spectrum estimates that one 40 kW rack would need about 80 m² of radiator [^48].

ABI Research's Andrew Cavalier told IEEE Spectrum that required radiator area grows about 40% after five years in orbit, and that orbital compute would cost at least ten times as much as a ground data center [^20].
US utility-scale solar ran at a 24.4% capacity factor in 2025 (preliminary) [^17].
On a per-panel DC basis it is roughly 19%, giving a 7.2x multiple.
Against a fixed-tilt panel at a cloudier mid-latitude site, at 11–15%, the multiple is 9–12x.
LBNL's *Queued Up* counts 2,061 GW of capacity waiting in US interconnection queues at end-2025, down from a peak near 2,600 GW at end-2023.
Energy itself is not expensive: US industrial electricity averaged 9.77¢/kWh in July 2026 [^28].
The only MEASURED number against that target is a bench demonstration in which one transceiver pair "achieved 800 Gbps each-way transmission (1.6 Tbps total)" over a short free-space path [^4,5].
The paper's own numbers make the point: a 2×2 spatially multiplexed array closes at about 1.25 km, and a 4×4 array only at about 0.32 km.
ESA counts about 40,000 tracked objects, about 11,000 of them active payloads at end-2024, plus more than 1.2 million objects larger than 1 cm.
Astronomer Jonathan McDowell counted 14,518 active payloads at end-January 2026, 9,555 of them Starlink [^47].
Starlink's reported collision-avoidance manoeuvres rose from about 50,000 in Dec 2023–May 2024 to 207,152 in Dec 2025–May 2026, as the fleet passed 10,000 satellites by June 2026 [^46].
The counts overstate risk in one respect: Starlink manoeuvres at a 3-in-10-million collision probability, far more conservative than NASA's common 1-in-10,000 threshold [^46].
An arXiv study of which workloads suit orbit scores LLM training 1 out of 5 on bandwidth and data locality [^50].
In 2021 dollars, the Space Shuttle cost about $65,400 per kilogram to low Earth orbit, while Falcon 9 brought that to about $2,600/kg and Falcon Heavy to about $1,500/kg [^26].
At a current reusable Falcon 9 price of roughly $3,600/kg, it puts launched power at $14,700/kW/yr.
It compares that with a terrestrial power spend of roughly $570–3,000/kW/yr [^5].
At full load that is about $856/kW/yr (ARA arithmetic: $0.0977 × 8,760 h), squarely inside Google's band.
As of 2026-02-27, SpaceX rideshare pricing was about $7,000/kg and rising, not falling [^27].
Epoch AI estimates a 1 GW AI datacenter at about $38B upfront, $26B of compute and $12B of construction.
Annualized, that is about $8.5B per year, of which servers account for roughly $5B, or 60% [^29].
Alphabet depreciates its servers over six years [^30].
Andrew McCalip, quoted by TechCrunch on how far optimistic and realistic assumptions diverge, put it bluntly: "This is not a 25% mismatch. It's 400%" [^22].
Fox Business reported that OpenAI's Sam Altman called orbital data centers "ridiculous" in "the current landscape" [^42].
| SemiAnalysis [^32] | $10.91 vs $2.49 per GPU-hour (~4.4x) after availability and redundancy |
| BCG [^33] | 20-year TCO of $660–750M/MW vs $230–300M/MW (2.5–3x); realistic path 1.5–1.8x |
| McCalip [^21] | $31.20/W vs $14.80/W for 1 GW over 5 years at $1,000/kg |
If in-orbit failure rates come in at the low end and launch reaches roughly $100–200/kg, BCG's realistic path narrows toward 1.5x.
But BCG's base case stays at a 2.5–3x premium even with launch near $100/kg [^33].
The operators claim 744 TOPS peak for the most capable satellite, 5 POPS across the 12 linked satellites, and laser links of up to 100 Gbps [^35].
In the company's words, its one-H100 satellite Starcloud-1 was "the first spacecraft to train an LLM - the nano GPT model from Andrej Karpathy."
Nvidia framed the payload as "100x more powerful GPU compute than any previous space-based operation" [^36].
Falcon 9 rideshare is "scheduled to end in 2028," and Starcloud-3 is planned to fly on Starship [^40].
The next step, Starcloud-2, is planned as two 8 kW satellites in 2027 [^40].
At a $2.3B valuation [^40].
Yet SpaceX's own IPO risk factors warn that the orbital data center plan "may not achieve commercial viability" [^51].
Starmind, its first compute satellite, so far exists only as an Nvidia announcement with a 2027 target [^41].
Axiom says its nodes perform commercial AI inferencing in orbit, a claim no third party has verified [^37].
On its Q3 FY2026 call, management described the work as "just an R&D at this phase. This is an R&D contract," covering "a couple of demo satellites" for Google [^11].
It is not contra revenue. It is contra R&D expense. [^12]
On its Q2 FY2027 call on 2026-09-09, it reported record revenue of $116M, roughly 58% growth, and 688 satellites launched on 42 rockets.
PL traded near $16.46 before the launch, per Benzinga [^15].
On 2026-10-02 it rose 7.8% to $17.44, which still left it 66.1% below its May 2026 52-week high of $51.40 [^16].
Alphabet raised its 2026 capital-expenditure guide to $195–205B from $180–190B and spent $44.9B in Q2 alone [^31].
| Sundar Pichai (Alphabet) | "a decade or so away we'll be viewing it as a more normal way to build data centers" | [^43] |
| Jeff Bezos (Blue Origin) | "We will be able to beat the cost of terrestrial data centres in space in the next couple of decades" | [^44] |
| Travis Beals (Suncatcher lead) | "I don't see this being something where it's cheaper to do this in the next five years" | [^6] |
SpaceX's FCC filing for up to 1M satellites argues that "within a few years the lowest cost to generate AI compute will be in space" [^38,47].
Google's paper implies about 49 W/kg for a Starlink v2-class satellite of 575 kg producing ~28 kW [^5].
Analyst Michael Pierce puts it plainly: "Training workloads likely cannot tolerate the synchronization and latency constraints of a distributed orbital system" [^48].
Planet's Mike Safyan made the same point to TechCrunch: "You're relying on very large radiators to just be able to dissipate that heat into the blackness of space" [^22].
